title: Reverse Proxy
description: Understand what Nginx and HAProxy do as reverse proxies — TLS termination, load balancing, caching, and compression — and why every production system needs one.

segments.text: Let's talk about the unsung hero sitting in front of every serious web application. The reverse proxy. You've heard of Nginx and HAProxy — today you'll understand exactly what they do and why.

A forward proxy sits in front of clients, hiding who's making the request. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers, hiding the backend infrastructure. Clients talk to the proxy, never knowing which server actually handled their request.

First superpower: TLS termination. The proxy handles all the expensive SSL handshakes and certificate management. Backend servers receive plain HTTP, saving them from cryptographic overhead. One place to manage certificates.

Second superpower: load balancing. The proxy distributes requests across backend servers. Round-robin, least connections, IP hash, weighted — different algorithms for different needs. If a server goes down, traffic routes around it automatically.
segments.thought_prompt: Why might you choose least-connections over simple round-robin?

segments.text: Third superpower: response caching. The proxy can cache responses and serve them directly without ever hitting your backend. Static assets, API responses with cache headers — all served at proxy speed.

Fourth superpower: compression. The proxy compresses responses with gzip or brotli before sending them over the network. Your backend sends uncompressed data locally, the proxy handles compression for the slow internet link.

The proxy also acts as a shield. Rate limiting stops abusive clients. Connection limits prevent any single user from hogging resources. It's your first line of defense against DDoS attacks and misbehaving clients.

Reverse proxies continuously ping backend servers with health checks. If a server stops responding, the proxy removes it from the pool within seconds. No manual intervention needed. Your users never see the failure.

Nginx excels at serving static content and is a great general-purpose proxy. HAProxy is purpose-built for load balancing with more advanced routing rules. Many production stacks use both — HAProxy in front, Nginx on each backend node.

Here's a common production layout. Internet traffic hits the load balancer, which forwards to multiple Nginx instances, each proxying to application servers. Every layer adds reliability and isolation.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens if the reverse proxy itself goes down? How would you make it highly available?

segments.text: The reverse proxy is not optional in production. TLS termination, load balancing, caching, compression, rate limiting, health checks — all handled before your application code even runs. It's the gatekeeper every system needs.
